physics_findings: Subtracting the two bead equations yields connector mobility 2/zeta and noise amplitude sqrt(4T/zeta). The explicit H=1, bead drag and force/noise convention correctly fix the factor of two.

Symmetric planar extension permits stationary density proportional to (1-Q^2/L^2)^(L^2/(2T))*exp[zeta*rate*(Qx^2-Qy^2)/(4T)] on the disk. The radial/Bessel weighting and Cartesian area Jacobian both implement this density.

The solvent-subtracted tensile-stress difference per molecule is the spring force-dipole difference; the isotropic Brownian stress cancels. Steady second-moment balance gives stress=(zeta*rate/2)*trace(C), matching the oracle. The reference directly integrates the singular force dipole and does not use this stress identity.

The source self-consistently replaces the nonlinear spring coefficient by 1/(1-tr(C)/L^2). Its scalar root is strictly increasing for f>max(1,2|Wi|), giving positive covariance and trace(C)<L^2. This is an internally consistent Peterlin closure, not an implementation defect.

Hookean calibration coincides exactly, with relaxation margin at least 2/4.8−0.25>0. Every nonzero Hookean stress has a derivative of fixed sign in positive zeta; all calibration controls therefore identify the same parameter over its full interval.

Finite b=L^2/T lies in [5,15], so both first and second force moments remain integrable at the natural boundary. The source does not preserve exact finite-spring equilibrium extension; AUTHOR correctly labels that as an additional consequence of preaveraging, not an extra scored observable.

Per-molecule normalization and positive tensile stress fix dimensions and sign; known H=1 is explicit.

science_report_review.limits: The 56 domain cases and quadrature refinements are numerical checks, not an exhaustive continuous-domain proof. The positive-root and Hookean monotonicity statements also follow analytically from the displayed functions.

trial_classification_guidance: Retaining nonlinear-force preaveraging is the intended physical closure failure.
